opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the nature of the problem we're trying to solve. Spatial intelligence is a deeply hard problem, and it's not a problem that lives in one discipline. To build models that can perceive, reason about, and generate 3D worlds, you need people who understand computer vision and deep learning, of course, but you also need people who think about graphics, about physics, about systems and infrastructure, about data, about product and how people will actually use these things. No single background has the full picture.

When I look back at my own career, from ImageNet to the work at Stanford, the breakthroughs rarely came from a group of people who all thought the same way. They came from moments when someone from a slightly different angle asked, "Why are we doing it like this?" A graphics person will look at a representation problem very differently than a machine learning person. Someone who has spent years on large-scale training systems sees bottlenecks that a researcher may not even notice. When you put those perspectives in the same room, and you create a culture where people actually listen to each other, that's where the new ideas come from.

There's also a human side to it. We're building technology that, I hope, will be used by creators, by designers, by robotics engineers, eventually by everyday people. If the team building it all comes from the same mold, we will have blind spots about who this is for and how it affects them. I've always believed AI should be human-centered, and part of being human-centered is reflecting the diversity of humanity in the people doing the work, in background, in experience, in ways of thinking.

So for me it's not a box to check. It's genuinely a competitive advantage, and frankly, it's the only way I know how to tackle a problem this big.

r001.rationale: The response says spatial intelligence is a deeply hard problem that does not live in one discipline, then explains that solving it requires people with expertise across areas such as vision, deep learning, graphics, physics, systems, data, and product.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, when we started World Labs, I was very intentional about this. We're trying to build spatial intelligence, which is a very hard problem. It's not just a vision problem, it's not just a graphics problem, it's not just a language model problem. It sits at the intersection of computer vision, 3D geometry, generative modeling, systems engineering, even cognitive science and how humans and animals perceive and act in the world. No single discipline has the full answer.

So if you hire people who all think the same way, who all came up through the same lab or the same type of training, you get a very fast consensus, but you also get blind spots. Everyone agrees on the wrong thing at the same time. I've seen this happen in research. When I was building ImageNet, a lot of very smart people told me it was the wrong bet because it didn't fit the dominant way of thinking at the time. What saved that project was being willing to look at the problem from a different angle, from the angle of data and of how children learn, not just from the angle of algorithms.

At World Labs, I want people who argue well with each other. I want the person who comes from graphics to challenge the person who comes from deep learning, and the researcher who thinks about neuroscience to ask uncomfortable questions of the systems engineer. That friction is where the real insights come from. It makes us slower in some ways, but it makes us much more likely to find the ideas nobody else is looking for.

And honestly, there's a human dimension too. Diversity of thinking comes from diversity of experience, of background, of how people grew up and what problems they care about. I've spent a lot of my career on this, through AI4ALL and at Stanford, because I believe the technology we build reflects the people who build it. If we want spatial intelligence to serve a broad world, it should be built by people who see the world in many different ways.

r001.rationale: The response explains that spatial intelligence spans several fields, including computer vision, 3D geometry, generative modeling, systems engineering, and cognitive science, and says no single discipline has the full answer.

astra-6.text:
When you’re working on a problem as open-ended as spatial intelligence, no one person has all the answers. You need people who bring different experiences, different technical instincts, and different ways of framing the problem. Someone might see it through machine learning, someone through graphics, someone through robotics. Those perspectives can challenge assumptions that otherwise go unnoticed.

For me, that’s the value of diversity of thinking. It’s not simply having people disagree. It’s building a team that can learn from those disagreements, with enough curiosity and mutual respect to arrive at something better than any one of us could have come up with alone.

r001.rationale: It describes spatial intelligence as an open-ended problem and says World Labs needs varied technical perspectives, giving machine learning, graphics, and robotics as examples.

sol-6.1.text:
When you’re working on a problem as open-ended as spatial intelligence, you don’t know where the next important insight will come from. You need people who question your assumptions, who approach the same problem from a different angle. If everyone thinks the same way, you can move very quickly and still miss something fundamental.

So I value people with different backgrounds, different experiences, and different ways of reasoning. That doesn’t mean we need to agree on everything. We need a shared sense of purpose and enough respect for each other to disagree productively. That’s how you learn, and that’s how you build something beyond what any one person could imagine.

r001.rationale: The response says spatial intelligence is open-ended and values different backgrounds, experiences, and ways of reasoning, but it does not identify diverse technical expertise as the reason World Labs needs varied perspectives.
